sentence: After four and a half years, one group showed no extra ageing.
claim: After 4.5 years, the daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin ageing; the relative odds of increased ageing in the daily vs discretionary group were 0.76 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.98), i.e. 24% less likely.
source_title: Hughes et al., Ann Intern Med 2013 (PubMed 23732711)
note: [SOURCE-READ] PubMed 23732711: 'The daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin aging after 4.5 years. Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).' (903 adults younger than 55 of the 1,621.)

sentence: In Nambour, Australia, pure chance decided who would wear sunscreen every morning.
claim: The Nambour Skin Cancer Prevention Trial (Queensland, Australia) randomly assigned 1,621 randomly selected adult residents of Nambour to daily or discretionary sunscreen use; the trial ran from 1992 to 1996 (February 1992 to August 1996 in one report).
source_title: Green et al., J Clin Oncol 2011 (PubMed 21135266)
note: [SOURCE-READ] PubMed 21135266 (efetch abstract, read 9 Nov): 'In 1992, 1,621 randomly selected residents of Nambour, a township in Queensland, Australia, age 25 to 75 years, were randomly assigned to daily or discretionary sunscreen application… until 1996.'

sentence: Head and arms, before the day began.
claim: The daily group applied SPF 15+ sunscreen to the head, neck, arms and hands every morning.
source_title: Green et al., J Clin Oncol 2011 (PubMed 21135266)
note: [SOURCE-READ] same abstract: 'daily or discretionary sunscreen application to head and arms'. The film now says 'Head and arms' (the old ledger's 'head, neck, arms and hands' came from a Lancet page not read).

sentence: The other group could use sunscreen whenever they liked.
claim: The control arm was not a no-sunscreen group: participants were randomised to daily sunscreen or to sunscreen use at their usual, discretionary rate, which allowed any use, including none.
source_title: Hughes et al., Ann Intern Med 2013 (PubMed 23732711)
note: [SOURCE-READ] PubMed 23732711 (Hughes 2013 abstract): 'regular use of sunscreen compared with discretionary use'; groups: 'daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreen…', 'discretionary use of sunscreen…'. Also PubMed 12707092 (Nambour, Arch Dermatol 2003).

sentence: Researchers then measured the fine lines on silicone copies of hands.
claim: Skin ageing was measured by skin microtopography: silicone impressions of the backs of participants' hands taken at baseline (1992) and 4.5 years later (1996), graded by assessors blinded to treatment group; 903 participants younger than 55.
source_title: Hughes et al., Ann Intern Med 2013 (PubMed 23732711)
note: [OPEN] PubMed 23732711 says 'Change in microtopography between 1992 and 1996… graded by assessors blinded to treatment allocation'. The abstract does not say 'silicone' (the old ledger's silicone impressions are from the full paper, not read): the voice says 'silicone copies of hands'; keep OPEN until a person checks the methods.

sentence: But an ultraviolet camera shows damage your eyes miss, long before it appears on the surface.
claim: UV photography shows sun damage that cannot be seen with the naked eye; extensive damage beneath the surface can build up long before signs show on the skin.
source_title: See how the sun damages your skin (American Academy of Dermatology)
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): AAD excerpts (via search): 'UV photography allows us to see sun damage that you cannot see with the naked eye'; AAD skin cancer page: 'long before you see signs on your skin, you can have extensive damage beneath the surface.' Cross-check: Gamble RG et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2012;67(4):587-97, UV photographs of 585 children aged 11–12; UV-photo sun damage was greatest in those with melanoma risk traits (all P < .001). Caveat from coverage: UV images show pigment changes, not cancer itself. The film's UV view is badged 'model'. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: Ten years later, they checked again.
claim: After the trial ended in 1996, participants were followed for about 10 more years (to 2006) for melanoma.
source_title: Green et al., J Clin Oncol 2011 (PubMed 21135266)
note: [SOURCE-READ] PubMed 21135266: 'Participants were observed until 2006… Ten years after trial cessation…'.

sentence: Melanoma, the most serious skin cancer, was about half as common in that group, though the numbers were small.
claim: Ten years after the trial ended, there were 11 primary melanomas in the daily group vs 22 in the discretionary group: hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.02; P = .051). Invasive melanoma: 3 vs 11, HR 0.27 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.97). Preinvasive: HR 0.73 (0.29 to 1.81).
source_title: Green et al., J Clin Oncol 2011 (PubMed 21135266)
note: [SOURCE-READ] PubMed 21135266: 'Ten years after trial cessation, 11 new primary melanomas had been identified in the daily sunscreen group, and 22 had been identified in the discretionary group… hazard ratio 0.50; 95% CI, 0.24 to 1.02; P = .051.' The count runs to 2006 (the plate says 'found by 2006'); 'not quite significant' is the film's wording for P = .051.

sentence: Melanoma, the most serious skin cancer, was about half as common in that group, though the numbers were small.
claim: Melanoma is the most serious (deadliest) form of skin cancer.
source_title: American Academy of Dermatology releases guidelines for melanoma treatment (AAD press release, Nov 2018, via Newswise)
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): Excerpts (via search): AAD 2018: 'melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer'; a 2023 AAD news item calls it 'the most serious form of skin cancer'. The film uses the AAD's newer, milder wording. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: At a lab's test dose, a layer of sunscreen is about a fifth as thick as a sheet of paper.
claim: SPF testing applies sunscreen at 2 mg/cm²; at a density of about 1 g/cm³ that is a film about 20 µm thick (16–17 µm for denser products), about a fifth of a ~100 µm sheet of paper (computed).
source_title: Submission to the TGA consultation on sunscreens (Antaria Ltd, hosted by the Therapeutic Goods Administration, Australia)
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): Excerpt (via search): 'if the application rate is 2 mg/cm2 and the density is 1 g/cm3, the film thickness is 0.0002 cm or 20 microns'; a 1.26 g/cm3 product gives about 16 microns. Another source puts 2 mg/cm² at 16.7 µm. 20 ÷ 100 = a fifth (computed); badged 'estimate'. This is the test dose, not what the trial measured; real-world layers are often thinner. Paper ≈ 100 µm: bible §6. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

claim: In the Nambour trial, the daily group applied sunscreen more often than the discretionary group, though neither group used it every day.
source_title: Daily sunscreen slowed skin aging in middle-aged adults (MDedge Family Medicine, 2013, on Hughes et al., Ann Intern Med 2013;158:781-790)
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): Excerpts (via search): 'By the end of the study, 77% of the daily sunscreen users applied sunscreen at least 3-4 days per week, vs. 33% of the discretionary users.' WBUR (4 Jun 2013) gives the same figures. 'Both' = the two model hands, standing for the two groups; 'missed mornings' follows from fewer than all of the daily group applying it even 3–4 days a week; 'one had more' = 77% vs 33%. The figures go on screen; confirm them in the paper's results. | Coordinator ruling (2 Nov): the 77% vs 33% figures came from coverage of Hughes 2013, not the paper itself; dropped from voice and screen unt A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: One missed fewer, and the skin kept count.
claim: The daily group had more sunscreen mornings than the discretionary group, and sun damage accumulates in skin over time, much of it before it can be seen.
source_title: See how the sun damages your skin (American Academy of Dermatology)
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): AAD excerpts (via search): 'the more sun damage we accumulate, the greater our risk of skin cancer and prematurely aged skin'; 'UV photography allows us to see sun damage that you cannot see with the naked eye.' 'Record' is a metaphor for that accumulation; the dermatologist checks it reads that way. 'Had more' = more mornings with sunscreen than the other group (Hughes 2013 adherence, see c12). 'Kept count' is a metaphor for accumulation; the dermatologist checks it reads that way and not as advice. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: Next: tanning beds share a list with cigarettes.
claim: IARC (the WHO's cancer agency) classifies UV-emitting tanning devices in Group 1, 'carcinogenic to humans', the same group as tobacco smoking (2009).
source_title: El Ghissassi F, et al. (WHO IARC Monograph Working Group). A review of human carcinogens, Part D: radiation. Lancet Oncol 2009;10:751–752
note: [OPEN] Carried over from the old ledger (old-3d/claims.json, search excerpts only; not page-read this session): The tease names No. 006's subject; the same source as No. 006's claim c2. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.
